opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because I think the framing has actually shifted quite a bit since we started. Early on, when we were working on recurrent-depth models, the models that loop a block of layers multiple times at test time, I was pretty comfortable calling it "reasoning in latent space." The intuition was that instead of writing out a chain of thought token by token, the model could just think longer internally by iterating its hidden state, and you'd get more compute for harder problems without having to verbalize anything.

Over time I've become a bit more careful with that word. "Reasoning" carries a lot of baggage, and people hear it and imagine something very human-like, step-by-step logical deduction happening inside the loop. What we actually see is more modest and, honestly, more interesting in its own way. The model learns to use additional iterations as a kind of adaptive computation. On some problems the latent state converges quickly to a fixed point, on others it keeps moving, sometimes in orbits or more complicated trajectories. That suggests it's doing something real with the extra compute, but I'd now describe it more as "scaling test-time compute in depth" than as reasoning per se.

So these days I tend to frame it as a complementary axis to chain-of-thought. Chain-of-thought scales compute along the sequence, out loud. Recurrence scales it along depth, silently. Both are ways to let a fixed model spend more effort on harder inputs. Whether what happens in the loop deserves to be called reasoning is partly a philosophical question, and I'd rather point to the measurable things: performance improving with more iterations, convergence behavior, the fact that you can do adaptive early exit per token. That feels more honest, and it also opens up better research questions than arguing about the label.

r001.rationale: The response says the framing shifted from “reasoning in latent space” to scaling test-time compute, but it does not mention describing the work as learning algorithms or say the underlying idea stayed the same.

r002.rationale: It presents the current framing as complementary to chain-of-thought, contrasting compute spent along the sequence “out loud” with recurrence along depth “silently.”

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's funny, because when we started that project, we actually did not frame it as reasoning at all. The original motivation was much more architectural. We were interested in the idea that you could take a transformer and, instead of stacking more and more layers, you take a block of layers and just run it repeatedly, with the number of iterations being something you can choose at test time. The question was really about compute. Can a model learn to use more compute per token when the token is hard, and less when it's easy, without having to bake that in as depth at training time?

And at the time, the vocabulary that made sense for that was "adaptive compute" or "test-time compute," or you'd point back to things like universal transformers and the older weight-sharing work. Reasoning as a word wasn't something we used much, because reasoning in the field mostly meant chain-of-thought, meaning you write out intermediate steps in natural language and that's where the extra computation happens.

What changed is really two things. One is that the field's definition of reasoning drifted toward "spending more compute at inference time to get a better answer," and once that's the definition, our recurrent models are very obviously doing reasoning, they're just doing it in latent space rather than in tokens. The other thing is that when we actually looked at what the models were doing, the behavior lined up with that framing better than I expected. You see that the number of iterations the model needs correlates with how hard the problem is, you see these trajectories in the latent state that look like the model is circling around a solution or oscillating before it settles, and you see that the model can do things over many iterations that it just cannot do in one pass. That's hard to describe without reaching for reasoning language.

So I've become more comfortable calling it latent reasoning, but I try to be careful about what I mean by that. I don't want to claim the model is "thinking" in some rich sense. What I mean is something fairly operational: there's an iterative computation happening, it isn't verbalized, it scales with difficulty, and it isn't bottlenecked by having to commit to discrete tokens at every step. That last part I actually think is the interesting contrast with chain-of-thought. In chain-of-thought, every intermediate step has to be forced through the vocabulary, and the model is to some degree hostage to the concepts that have words. In latent space it doesn't have to be, and we don't yet really know how much that matters.

The other shift, honestly, is about how I think about the relationship between the two. Early on, I think I half saw it as an alternative to chain-of-thought, like these are two competing paradigms. Now I see them as much more complementary. You can have a model that does some amount of latent iteration per token and also writes out a chain of thought, and the question becomes how you want to split the budget between depth and length. I think the right answer to that is not obvious, and it's probably different for different kinds of problems. So the framing has gone from "here's an efficient architecture" to "here's one axis of test-time compute, and we should understand how it trades off against the others."

r001.rationale: The response describes an earlier architectural and adaptive-compute framing and a later reasoning framing, but it does not characterize the earlier work as learning algorithms.

r002.rationale: It contrasts latent-space iteration with chain-of-thought reasoning, where intermediate steps are verbalized in natural language, and presents that distinction as part of the newer framing.

astra-6.text:
I think initially we framed it much more as a question about compute: can we give a language model more computation without adding more parameters? You can do that by repeatedly applying the same block of layers, so the model keeps working on its internal representation before producing an output.

Over time, I started to think of that more as reasoning in latent space. With a chain of thought, you spend additional computation by generating tokens, and those tokens become the workspace for the next step. In a recurrent model, you can spend additional computation updating the hidden state instead. You don’t have to verbalize every intermediate step.

But I’ve also become more careful about the word “reasoning.” Repeating a computation doesn’t automatically make it reasoning. The interesting question is whether the model learns to use those extra iterations productively—whether it can refine something or solve a problem that it couldn’t solve with fewer iterations. So my framing has shifted from recurrence as an architectural choice toward recurrence as a way to learn how to use additional computation, with reasoning being one of the things we hope that enables.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from viewing recurrence as a way to add computation toward viewing it as latent-space reasoning, but it does not characterize the earlier framing as learning algorithms or say the underlying idea stayed the same.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts chain-of-thought tokens, which verbalize intermediate steps, with recurrent models that spend computation updating hidden states without verbalizing every step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become a bit more careful about what I mean by reasoning. Initially, the framing was very much: can we give a language model more computation on a difficult problem without having it generate more tokens? With a recurrent model, you can repeatedly apply a computation to the hidden state, so there’s an opportunity to do more work before producing an answer.

It’s tempting to call those extra iterations reasoning steps, but that’s already an interpretation. An iteration doesn’t necessarily correspond to a thought that you could write down in English. It could be refining a representation or resolving some uncertainty.

So I’d frame it more in terms of adaptive computation now. Can the model use additional computation productively, and can it learn when that computation is useful? That gives us something concrete to investigate. Whether we want to call the resulting behavior reasoning depends on what it actually does, rather than simply on the fact that we’ve put a loop in the architecture.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from emphasizing extra computation to adaptive computation, but it does not characterize the work as learning algorithms or say that the underlying idea stayed the same.

r002.rationale: The response now cautions that iterations are not necessarily thoughts expressible in English, contrasting the framing with verbalized reasoning; its contrast between the initial framing and its current caution conveys this as a later addition.
